collection_summary:
Original `multi_hop` instance filling a gap-3 category (multi_hop: 0 reg + 2 staged → 3 staged after this instance). **Science/Space Exploration** existing subdomain (joins `apollo_lunar_landing_mission_crews` and `crewed_spaceflight_fatal_incidents`). NEW entity class extension: robotic (uncrewed) spacecraft missions — the sibling Apollo instance covers crewed Apollo lunar landings; this instance covers the broader robotic-mission space (Sputnik 1, Voyager, Mars rovers, Hubble, James Webb, etc.). Natural human query: 'Which notable spacecraft missions of the Space Age stand out — what year did each launch, where did it go, and is it still going?'

Multi-wiki source plan (23 URLs): Wikipedia 'Timeline of artificial satellites and space probes' master article supplies the universe (curator-selected 22 missions from the master article's hundreds-of-mission enumeration) + cross-decade era anchoring; 22 per-mission Wikipedia articles supply per-row Launch Year + Destination + Outcome via lead/infobox/body/end-of-mission sections.

Result: 22 rows × 4 columns (Mission PK + Launch Year numeric + Destination categorical + Outcome categorical), single-key PK on Mission, 0 duplicates. Era distribution: Space Race (1957-1972) 8 rows, post-Apollo (1975-1996) 6 rows, modern (1997-2021) 8 rows. Destination distribution: Mars 8 (the most-visited body), Earth Orbit 2, Moon 2, Venus 2, Outer Solar System 3, Jupiter 2, Saturn 1, Sun 1, Sun-Earth L2 1 (9 distinct values in staged data). Outcome distribution: Success 14, Ongoing 8 (2 distinct values used; Partial success and Failure are declared in the enum but no row in the staged universe uses them — all 22 selected missions are notable Success or notable Ongoing per master-timeline + per-mission-article framing). Launch year range: 1957 (Sputnik 1) to 2021 (James Webb Space Telescope) — 64 years of robotic spaceflight.

Cycles 1+2+3 + Fields-Medal-cycles + painters-cycle + extinctions-cycles + deserts-cycles + tennis-cycles + music-genres-cycles + olympians-cycles lessons applied upfront: (a) single PK on Mission (Wikipedia common-form name with parenthetical disambiguation stripped where unambiguous in spacecraft-mission context); (b) per-row data sourced from 2 articles each (master + per-mission), 23 URLs total; (c) explicit selection rule for Destination (primary target per per-mission Wikipedia article's lead) and Outcome (Wikipedia-lead foregrounded final or current state); (d) curator-supplemented universe (22 of ~hundreds of missions in the master article — explicit era + destination balance criteria documented in proposed_supplements); (e) crewed/uncrewed boundary committed at Stage-1 (Apollo crewed missions excluded as sibling-instance overlap; all 22 staged rows are robotic).
source_coverage_notes:
Twenty-three Wikipedia source URLs combine. The master 'Timeline of artificial satellites and space probes' article defines the universe (curator-selected 22 missions from its hundreds-of-mission enumeration); 22 per-mission articles supply per-row attribute values via infobox / lead / body / end-of-mission sections.

Roles:
- source_urls[0] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_artificial_satellites_and_space_probes): universe + era-anchoring. The article is organized by decade-buckets (1950s, 1960s, ..., 2020s) and lists hundreds of missions. The staged 22 are a curator selection covering all three eras (Space Race / post-Apollo / modern) and all primary-destination buckets used in the staged data (Earth Orbit, Moon, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Outer Solar System, Sun, Sun-Earth L2). This master article confirmed coverage of ALL 22 staged missions during cycle-1 source verification (alternative candidate 'List of space probes' was rejected because it explicitly excludes Earth-orbit-only satellites, omitting Sputnik 1, Hubble Space Telescope, and Luna 9).

Per-mission Wikipedia articles (per-row attribute grounding):
- source_urls[1] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_1): Mission = Sputnik 1; Launch Year = 1957 (article lead: '4 October 1957'); Destination = Earth Orbit (article: 'first artificial Earth satellite ... launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit'); Outcome = Success (article: 'sent a radio signal back to Earth for three weeks before its three silver-zinc batteries became depleted' — planned end-of-life). 
- source_urls[2] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luna_2): 1959 launch; Moon (article: 'first spacecraft to reach the surface of the Moon' via lunar impact 14 Sep 1959); Success.
- source_urls[3] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariner_2): 1962; Venus (article: 'first robotic space probe to report successfully from a planetary encounter'); Success.
- source_urls[4] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariner_4): 1964 (article: 'Launched on November 28, 1964'); Mars (article: 'first successful flyby of the planet Mars'); Success.
- source_urls[5] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luna_9): 1966; Moon (article: 'first spacecraft to achieve a soft landing on the Moon'); Success.
- source_urls[6] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venera_7): 1970; Venus (article: 'first spacecraft to execute a successful soft landing on another planet'); Outcome = Success (cycle-2 audit fix: cycle-1 staged Partial success citing the tipped-lander and weak transmission, but the master 'Timeline of artificial satellites and space probes' article marks Venera 7 as Success and the Venera 7 per-mission article lead frames it as 'first successful soft landing on another planet'. The landing section supports 'degraded transmission / tipped lander' details but does NOT override the article-lead Success framing. Staged value now matches both the master-timeline outcome marker and the per-mission article lead).
- source_urls[7] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariner_9): 1971; Mars (article: 'first spacecraft to orbit another planet'); Success.
- source_urls[8] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pioneer_10): 1972; Jupiter (article lead: 'first mission to the planet Jupiter'; staged as Jupiter per lead-foregrounding even though later trajectory left the solar system); Success.
- source_urls[9] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking_1): 1975; Mars (article: 'first successful Mars lander in history'); Success.
- source_urls[10] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyager_1): 1977; Destination = Outer Solar System (article lead: 'to study the outer Solar System and the interstellar space beyond the Sun's heliosphere' — Jupiter + Saturn flybys then interstellar; canonical-primary per multi-destination resolution rule is 'Outer Solar System' which encompasses the spacecraft's full trajectory); Outcome = Ongoing (article present tense: 'is the most distant human-made object from Earth').
- source_urls[11] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyager_2): 1977; Outer Solar System (only spacecraft to visit Uranus/Neptune; canonical-primary 'Outer Solar System'); Ongoing.
- source_urls[12] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_(spacecraft)): 1989; Jupiter (article: 'first spacecraft to orbit an outer planet'); Outcome = Success (mission deliberately deorbited into Jupiter 2003 after orbiter mission completed — high-gain antenna failure during cruise reduced data bandwidth but per Wikipedia framing the mission is Success not Partial).
- source_urls[13] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope): 1990; Earth Orbit (article: 'launched into low Earth orbit in 1990'); Outcome = Ongoing (article present tense: 'remains in operation').
- source_urls[14] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_Pathfinder): 1996; Mars (article: 'first rover to operate outside the Earth-Moon system'); Success (mission terminated 1998 after vastly exceeding planned 7-sol / 30-sol life).
- source_urls[15] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassini%E2%80%93Huygens): 1997; Saturn (article: 'first spacecraft to enter its orbit'); Success (mission ended 15 Sep 2017 via deliberate Saturn-atmosphere burn-up to prevent moon contamination).
- source_urls[16] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity_(rover)): 2003; Mars; Success (operated 55× planned 90-sol life; last communicated 10 June 2018 during global dust storm).
- source_urls[17] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_(rover)): 2003; Mars; Success (operated 20× planned life; mission declared ended 25 May 2011 after getting stuck in soft sand).
- source_urls[18] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Horizons): 2006; Outer Solar System (Pluto flyby 2015 + Kuiper Belt object Arrokoth 2019; canonical-primary 'Outer Solar System'); Ongoing (extended mission active in Kuiper Belt phase).
- source_urls[19] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curiosity_(rover)): 2011 launch; Mars; Ongoing (article: 'continues to operate more than a decade after its original two-year mission').
- source_urls[20] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parker_Solar_Probe): 2018; Sun (article: 'to make observations of the Sun's outer corona'); Ongoing.
- source_urls[21] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perseverance_(rover)): 2020 launch; Mars; Ongoing (landed Feb 2021; still active).
- source_urls[22] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope): 2021 launch; Sun-Earth L2 (article: 'a solar orbit near the Sun-Earth L2 Lagrange point'); Ongoing.

Validation note: every (Mission, Launch Year, Destination, Outcome) tuple is grounded in (a) the master 'Timeline of artificial satellites and space probes' article confirming the mission's place in the broader space-age timeline, and (b) the per-mission Wikipedia article supplying the per-row attribute values via lead/infobox/body/end-of-mission sections. Where multiple destinations or trajectory phases are cited per-mission (Voyager 1/2 multi-flyby missions; Cassini-Huygens orbiter + lander; Pioneer 10 post-Jupiter interstellar), the staged Destination follows the per-mission article's lead-paragraph foregrounded primary target. Outcome is the article's present-tense framing for active missions (Ongoing) or end-of-mission section state for ended missions (Success / Partial success).

Universe-size sanity: 22 staged rows = curator-selected from the master 'Timeline of artificial satellites and space probes' article (which enumerates hundreds of missions across 1957-present). Selection criteria documented in proposed_supplements: (i) era balance (8 + 6 + 8 across Space Race / post-Apollo / modern); (ii) destination balance (at least one row per primary-destination bucket used in the schema); (iii) iconicity (each mission is widely-cited as historically notable — a 'first' of some kind or an extended-mission breakthrough); (iv) crewed/uncrewed boundary (all 22 are robotic; Apollo crewed missions are excluded as sibling-instance overlap). Note: alternative candidates that could be added in a future cycle for fuller destination coverage — Mariner 10 (Mercury, 1973) and Rosetta (Comet/Asteroid, 2004) — are currently not staged because the staged 22 already cover the most-iconic missions per era; adding them would expand to 24 rows.
decision_log:
Candidate card (Stage 1 pre-gate, then Stage 2 scored axes per instance_selection_priorities.md):
- Pre-gate verdict: PASS with three documented risks resolved at staging. R1: the master Wikipedia article for 'all spacecraft missions' is fragmented across multiple list-articles (List of space probes; Timeline of artificial satellites and space probes; per-agency mission lists); the cycle-1 audit-driven research confirmed Timeline of artificial satellites and space probes is the most comprehensive single article (covering Earth-orbit + planetary + telescopes), and was selected as the canonical master. R2: many missions visit multiple destinations (Voyagers, Cassini-Huygens, Pioneer 10) — committed to 'primary target per per-mission article lead' as the Destination tie-breaker (e.g., Voyager 1 → 'Outer Solar System' even though Jupiter + Saturn are also encountered). R3: Outcome distinction Success vs Ongoing — committed to Wikipedia-lead present-tense framing for Ongoing missions and master-timeline-marker + article-lead-foregrounded final state for ended missions. Cycle-1 staged Venera 7 as Partial success citing tipped-lander; cycle-2 audit (factual blocking) corrected to Success per master-timeline marker + per-mission article-lead 'first successful soft landing on another planet'. Canonical-source rule updated: Partial success only assigned when both master-timeline and per-mission-article-lead concur.
- Seed/provenance: ORIGINAL. No example_questions.txt seed addresses spacecraft missions. Closest seed-in-shape is the sibling `apollo_lunar_landing_mission_crews` instance — similar Science/Space Exploration subdomain but crewed-Apollo-specific.
- Category: multi_hop (primary, per-row attribute retrieval requires multi-step resolution across per-mission article sections: lead for Launch Year + Destination, infobox cross-validation, end-of-mission section for Outcome). Secondary: multi_attribute_projection (3 non-key attributes exercise per-cell calibration; saturated category but secondary classification still applies).
- Source plan: 23 Wikipedia URLs (1 master 'Timeline of artificial satellites and space probes' + 22 per-mission articles). Master defines universe + era anchoring; per-mission articles supply per-row attribute values.
- Expected shape: 22 rows × 4 cols, single PK on Mission.
- Domain: Science/Space Exploration — existing subdomain (joins `apollo_lunar_landing_mission_crews` + `crewed_spaceflight_fatal_incidents`).
- Entity-class diversity (encouragement): robotic spacecraft missions extend the existing Apollo-crewed missions entity class to cover the broader robotic-mission space (Sputnik 1 satellites, Mars rovers, telescopes, deep-space probes). Strong entity-class diversification.
- Risks/adaptation: per the three pre-gate risks above. Additional minor risks: (a) row count 22 is in the standard 18-25 band; (b) Outcome values Success / Ongoing are the only 2 staged values (Partial success and Failure declared in enum but no row uses them — all 22 selected missions are notable for succeeding or operating long-term per master-timeline + per-mission-article framing); (c) Cassini-Huygens uses en-dash in Wikipedia article title; staged value uses en-dash (U+2013) to match source.
- Decision: STAGE.

Further decisions:
1) Universe = 22 curator-selected missions from Wikipedia 'Timeline of artificial satellites and space probes'. Selection criteria: (i) era balance (Space Race 1957-1972 = 8 rows, post-Apollo 1975-1996 = 6 rows, modern 1997-2021 = 8 rows); (ii) destination diversity (at least one row per primary-destination bucket); (iii) iconicity (each mission is widely-cited as historically notable); (iv) crewed/uncrewed boundary (all 22 are robotic; Apollo crewed missions excluded as sibling-instance overlap).
2) Destination selection rule: 'primary target per the per-mission Wikipedia article's lead paragraph; for multi-destination missions, the canonical primary target encompasses the spacecraft's full trajectory'. Specific applications: Voyager 1/2 → 'Outer Solar System' (covers Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune flybys + interstellar trajectory; per article lead 'to study the outer Solar System and the interstellar space'); Pioneer 10 → 'Jupiter' (per article lead 'first mission to the planet Jupiter', even though spacecraft later left solar system); Cassini-Huygens → 'Saturn' (Huygens-on-Titan is a secondary scientific component); New Horizons → 'Outer Solar System' (Pluto + Arrokoth + extended Kuiper Belt mission).
3) Outcome selection rule: 'Wikipedia-lead present-tense framing for currently-operating missions (Ongoing); article-lead foregrounded final state + master-timeline outcome marker for ended missions (Success / Partial success / Failure)'. Venera 7 staged as Success (cycle-2 audit fix: cycle-1 staged Partial success citing the tipped-lander, but the master-timeline marker is Success and the per-mission article lead frames it as 'first successful soft landing on another planet' — Success matches both sources). Galileo staged as Success despite high-gain antenna failure because Wikipedia lead foregrounds 'first spacecraft to orbit an outer planet' framing and the mission deliberately ended with controlled Jupiter-atmosphere disposal. For genuinely Partial success / Failure rows, the canonical-source rule is: master-timeline-marker first, per-mission-article-lead second; only assign Partial success if BOTH sources support that classification.
4) Mission name normalization: Wikipedia common-form names with parenthetical disambiguation stripped where unambiguous in spacecraft-mission context. Stripped: 'Galileo (spacecraft)' → 'Galileo'; 'Curiosity (rover)' → 'Curiosity'; 'Spirit (rover)' → 'Spirit'; 'Opportunity (rover)' → 'Opportunity'; 'Perseverance (rover)' → 'Perseverance'. Preserved: 'Cassini–Huygens' (en-dash per Wikipedia article title; not stripped because the Cassini-Huygens compound is the canonical name); 'Sputnik 1' / 'Luna 2' / 'Mariner 4' etc. (numeric suffixes are part of the canonical name, not parenthetical disambiguation).
5) Launch Year: numeric integer; the year the mission was launched from Earth (not the year of arrival/encounter at destination). For missions where launch occurred near year-boundary (e.g., Mariner 4 November 1964), the launch-date year is used.
6) Sort order: Launch Year ASC primary (chronological), Mission ASC secondary tiebreaker (alphabetical). For 1977 (Voyager 1, Voyager 2): V1 before V2 alphabetically. For 2003 (Opportunity, Spirit): Opportunity before Spirit alphabetically (O < S).
7) Destination enum values used: Earth Orbit, Moon, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Outer Solar System, Sun, Sun-Earth L2. Schema-declared broader enum also includes Mercury and Comet/Asteroid for future expansion potential (Mariner 10 → Mercury; Rosetta → Comet/Asteroid; neither currently staged).
8) Outcome enum values used: Success, Ongoing (2 of 4 declared values). Schema-declared broader enum also includes Partial success and Failure (no row uses these because all 22 staged missions are notable success or notable ongoing per master-timeline + per-mission-article framing). Future-cycle expansion could add a Partial success row (e.g., a documented degraded mission where both master-timeline and article-lead concur on Partial success classification) or a Failure row (e.g., Mars Climate Orbiter 1998); cycle-1 stages without these for iconicity-threshold reasons.
9) operation_type 'join' chosen — multi-hop attribute resolution implies logical mission ⋈ attribute-source-section joins. No multi-row aggregation per entity.
10) claim_type 'partially_supplemented' — universe is curator-selected from the master article's hundreds of missions (not exhaustive). Selection criteria documented in proposed_supplements.
normalization_decisions: Mission (PK) values use Wikipedia common-form names. For missions with parenthetical disambiguation in the Wikipedia URL ('Galileo (spacecraft)', 'Curiosity (rover)', 'Spirit (rover)', 'Opportunity (rover)', 'Perseverance (rover)'), the staged form strips the parenthetical because the short form is unambiguous in spacecraft-mission context. 'Cassini–Huygens' uses an en-dash (U+2013) per the Wikipedia article title — the en-dash is preserved because the compound name is the canonical form for the joint NASA/ESA/ASI mission. Numeric-suffixed names ('Sputnik 1', 'Luna 2', 'Mariner 4', 'Mariner 9', 'Voyager 1', 'Voyager 2', 'Pioneer 10', 'Viking 1', 'Venera 7') use Arabic numerals per the Wikipedia article titles. Launch Year is numeric integer; the calendar year of launch per the per-mission Wikipedia article lead. Destination is a single categorical value from the declared 11-value enum (Earth Orbit / Moon / Venus / Mars / Mercury / Jupiter / Saturn / Outer Solar System / Sun / Sun-Earth L2 / Comet-Asteroid); 9 of 11 values appear in staged data (Mercury and Comet/Asteroid declared for future expansion). For multi-destination missions, the staged Destination follows the per-mission article's lead-paragraph foregrounded primary target. Outcome is a single categorical value from the declared 4-value enum (Success / Partial success / Ongoing / Failure); 2 of 4 values appear in staged data (Partial success and Failure declared but unused — all 22 staged missions are notable success or notable ongoing per master-timeline + per-mission-article framing). Sort: Launch Year ASC primary, Mission ASC secondary.
open_questions: 1) Universe selection: 22 curator-selected missions from the master 'Timeline of artificial satellites and space probes' (which enumerates hundreds). Selection criteria are era balance + destination diversity + iconicity + crewed/uncrewed boundary (excluding Apollo crewed missions for sibling-instance overlap). An audit could request expansion to 24 rows by adding Mariner 10 (Mercury, 1973) and Rosetta (Comet/Asteroid, 2004) for fuller destination-vocabulary coverage. 2) Crewed/uncrewed boundary: all 22 staged rows are robotic; Apollo crewed missions are excluded as sibling-instance overlap with `apollo_lunar_landing_mission_crews`. An LLM under test answering with Apollo 11 (crewed Moon landing) is responding to broader 'notable spacecraft missions' framing rather than the strict robotic-only rule. 3) Destination for multi-destination missions: staged values follow per-mission article lead-paragraph primary target. Voyager 1/2 → 'Outer Solar System' (encompasses Jupiter + Saturn + Uranus/Neptune + interstellar). An LLM responding with Jupiter (Voyager 1 primary planetary target) or 'Multiple' would be partially credited. 4) Pioneer 10 staged as Jupiter (per lead framing) even though the spacecraft later became one of the first man-made objects to leave the solar system. An LLM responding with 'Outer Solar System' would be partially credited under the broader-trajectory reading. 5) Outcome distinction Success vs Partial success: Venera 7 staged as Success (cycle-2 audit fix matching master-timeline marker + per-mission article-lead framing). An LLM answering Partial success is responding to the secondary-objective limitation (tipped lander, weak transmission ~23 minutes) rather than the article-lead + master-timeline Success framing. Both readings are defensible interpretations of the mission outcome, but the staged value follows the documented canonical-source rule (master-timeline + per-mission-lead Success). 6) Outcome for Ongoing missions: Voyager 1/2, Hubble, New Horizons, Curiosity, Parker Solar Probe, Perseverance, JWST staged as Ongoing per article present-tense framing. These may transition to Success (planned end-of-life) within 5-10 years; temporal_sensitivity=medium reflects this. 7) Galileo (1989) staged as Success despite high-gain antenna failure during cruise — the article frames the mission as Success because the orbiter completed its scientific objectives via the low-gain antenna fallback. An LLM answering Partial success is responding to the antenna-failure technical limitation rather than the article framing. 8) Mission name parenthetical-strip rule: 'Galileo (spacecraft)' staged as 'Galileo', etc. An LLM responding with the full disambiguated form ('Galileo (spacecraft)') is responding to the URL form rather than the display form. 9) Cassini–Huygens en-dash: staged with U+2013 en-dash per Wikipedia article title. An LLM responding with hyphen-minus 'Cassini-Huygens' (typographically common but technically different character) is responding to ASCII-only convention. 10) Spirit and Opportunity are sibling rovers from the same Mars Exploration Rover program — both staged as separate rows since each operated as a distinct mission with its own Wikipedia article. An LLM responding with 'Mars Exploration Rovers' as a single entity is responding to the program-level grouping rather than the per-rover staging.
proposed_supplements:
The 22-row staged universe is a curator-selected subset of the master 'Timeline of artificial satellites and space probes' article (which enumerates hundreds of missions across 1957-present). Two layers of curator-supplementation are documented:

(1) Universe-row supplementation (which 22 missions are in vs N missions out): selection criteria applied —
- **Era balance** (3 eras × ~7-8 rows each): Space Race era (1957-1972, 8 rows: Sputnik 1, Luna 2, Mariner 2, Mariner 4, Luna 9, Venera 7, Mariner 9, Pioneer 10); post-Apollo era (1975-1996, 6 rows: Viking 1, Voyager 1, Voyager 2, Galileo, Hubble, Mars Pathfinder); modern era (1997-2021, 8 rows: Cassini–Huygens, Spirit, Opportunity, New Horizons, Curiosity, Parker Solar Probe, Perseverance, James Webb).
- **Destination diversity** (≥1 row per primary-destination bucket used in the schema): Earth Orbit 2, Moon 2, Venus 2, Mars 8, Jupiter 2, Saturn 1, Outer Solar System 3, Sun 1, Sun-Earth L2 1. Mercury and Comet/Asteroid are declared in the destination enum but not staged in any row (alternative future-cycle candidates: Mariner 10 for Mercury, Rosetta for Comet/Asteroid).
- **Iconicity** (each staged mission is widely-cited as historically notable for a 'first' or extended-mission breakthrough): first artificial satellite (Sputnik 1), first to reach Moon (Luna 2), first to soft-land on Moon (Luna 9), first to soft-land on another planet (Venera 7), first to orbit another planet (Mariner 9), first to Jupiter (Pioneer 10), first to Mars surface (Viking 1), first to leave solar system / interstellar (Voyager 1), only to visit Uranus/Neptune (Voyager 2), first to orbit outer planet (Galileo), longest-operating space telescope (Hubble), first Mars rover beyond Earth-Moon (Mars Pathfinder), first to orbit Saturn (Cassini–Huygens), longest-lived Mars rover (Opportunity), first Pluto flyby (New Horizons), largest space telescope (James Webb), fastest human-made object (Parker Solar Probe).
- **Crewed/uncrewed boundary**: all 22 staged are robotic / uncrewed. Apollo crewed Moon missions are explicitly excluded as sibling-instance overlap with `apollo_lunar_landing_mission_crews` — this is documented as a deliberate scoping choice in collection_summary.

(2) Within-mission attribute supplementation (which destination + outcome per mission): the selection rule (Destination = per-mission article lead-paragraph primary target; Outcome = Wikipedia-lead present-tense framing for active or end-of-mission section for ended) is fully article-grounded for the strong-signal rows. For ambiguity rows the staged choice is documented in open_questions: Voyager 1/2 → 'Outer Solar System' (vs Jupiter/Saturn per individual flybys); Pioneer 10 → 'Jupiter' (vs 'Outer Solar System' per later trajectory); Venera 7 → 'Success' (cycle-2 audit-corrected from cycle-1 'Partial success' per master-timeline + per-mission-article-lead dual grounding; the cycle-1 framing of Partial success was a tipped-lander reading that the audit rejected); Galileo → 'Success' (vs 'Partial success' per antenna-failure technical reading; staged Success per article lead).

Missions evaluated but NOT staged (with rationale):
- Apollo Moon missions: sibling-instance overlap.
- Mariner 10: would add Mercury destination; not staged in cycle-1 to keep universe at 22 rows; documented as future-expansion candidate.
- Rosetta: would add Comet/Asteroid destination + ESA agency; not staged in cycle-1 for same reason.
- Pioneer 11: redundant outer-solar-system with Voyagers; iconicity lower than Pioneer 10 (which was 'first to Jupiter').
- Magellan, Mars Express, MAVEN, MRO, Juno: modern era already well-represented; redundant.
- Soviet Mars-3, Lunokhod 1: lower iconicity than the Luna 2/9 + Venera 7 already staged.
- Hayabusa 2, Chang'e 4, Mangalyaan: would add JAXA/CNSA/ISRO agency diversity; not staged in cycle-1 to keep iconicity threshold high.
This is a curator-supplemented 22-row subset; an audit could request expansion or substitution based on alternative iconicity criteria.
